endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Use formats and languages accessible to intended end users | Multiple formats (text, video, audio) and languages (English, Chinese, Swahili)

endorsements.title: Training for tomorrow: Establishing a worldwide curriculum in online adaptive radiation therapy
endorsements.issuer: Technical innovations & patient support in radiation oncology
endorsements.quote: Further, the design and delivery of oART training for a global audience may benefit from a modular approach tailored to regional needs.

commentary.bottom_line: Two sources endorse delivering AI training in multiple formats and languages, but no supplied study tests whether doing so improves user understanding, safe use, or patient outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and commentary alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests accessible training formats, and no study documents the hazard of inaccessible formats. The support consists of one consensus guideline and one commentary. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an effect estimate, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The FUTURE-AI guideline names English, Chinese, and Swahili as example languages, and the radiation therapy commentary suggests modules tailored to regional needs. Neither source reports data on whether users with limited English proficiency or low literacy were reached or whether their use of AI changed as a result.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study measures whether multi-format or multilingual AI training changes clinician or staff comprehension, appropriate reliance on AI output, error rates, or patient outcomes compared with single-format training. Studies are also needed that document how often current training formats exclude intended users and which user groups are affected.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these populations have no direct evidence on which training formats work for their staff or for patient-facing users, and any adoption would proceed on consensus alone.
